analysis.one_liner: Makes school breakfast and lunch free for every child, regardless of family income.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended, despite 18 Democratic sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made school breakfast and lunch free for all children, eliminating the income-application process and the reduced-price tier entirely. It would have raised federal reimbursement rates for schools, banned 'lunch shaming' practices like separating kids with unpaid meal debt or marking them with tokens, prohibited schools from collecting unpaid meal debt, and reimbursed schools for existing delinquent meal debt. It also expanded free summer meals to all children, created a $60-per-child-per-month summer grocery card for low-income households, and rewrote how schools count low-income students for education funding.
analysis.who_benefits: All families with school-age children, who stop paying for meals and applying for benefits; families with unpaid meal debt, who stop owing it; schools, which get higher reimbursement rates and forgiveness of delinquent debt; and low-income households, who get summer grocery benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Provides free breakfast and lunch to all school children regardless of income, eliminating the income-eligibility application and the reduced-price tier.
Prohibits schools from physically segregating or identifying children who receive free meals, and bars schools from collecting debt for unpaid meal charges.

Raises the federal reimbursement rate to $2.72 per breakfast and $3.81 per lunch, adjusted for inflation, with an extra 30 cents per lunch for schools serving meals with locally sourced farm products.
Expands the summer food service program to all children and creates a Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer program giving low-income households $60 per month per child during summer months.

Reimburses schools for all existing delinquent meal debt and redefines the poverty measure for federal education funding to directly count homeless, foster, migratory, and public-benefit-receiving children.
Extends free lunch eligibility to juveniles incarcerated in public juvenile detention centers.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through appropriations the bill authorizes in unlimited amounts ('such sums as may be necessary'), with the universal expansion largely replacing meal fees families used to pay.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes spending without a cost estimate or spending cap, relying on open-ended appropriations ('such sums as may be necessary') for the summer EBT program and by implication for the whole program.
Free meals for all children deliver federal dollars to higher-income families who already pay for school meals, rather than concentrating resources on the poorest households.
School districts lose paid-lunch and paid-breakfast fee revenue, and the bill assumes federal reimbursement rates set in the text will fully cover the cost of universal free meals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and concrete: tens of millions of children get free meals, the poorest get summer grocery cards, and humiliating debt-collection practices end. The honest cost is a major increase in federal food spending, and some of that money goes to families who don't need help paying for lunch. The design choices (universal eligibility, open-ended funding) make it a bigger and less targeted program than an income-tested expansion would be.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees in October 2019, then to a subcommittee in November, and no committee ever took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the Universal School Meals Program Act of 2019 in the House on October 15, 2019, with six original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Education and Labor, Agriculture, and Science, Space, and Technology Committees, none of which reported it out.
On November 8, 2019 it was referred to a subcommittee on nutrition within the Agriculture committee, and the action history shows no further activity for the rest of the Congress.
The bill ended the 116th Congress with 17 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, never having received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No constituency gained; the bill simply expired in committee. Families continued paying for and applying for school meals, and schools continued collecting unpaid meal debt under the pre-existing rules.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; with Democrats holding the House majority, the committees that never acted were also chaired by Democrats.

industries.note: Universal free meals plus higher reimbursement rates would increase the number of federally paid meals these companies prepare under contract to districts, and the bill reimburses districts for previously uncollected meal debt. Their gain comes through expanded federal funding, alongside the public benefit.

industries.industry: Agriculture, especially local and regional farm suppliers
industries.note: The bill pays schools an extra 30 cents per lunch for serving meals made from locally sourced farm products, creating a new market channel for farms within 250 miles of a school.

industries.industry: School districts and school meal programs
industries.note: Districts get higher federal reimbursement rates, forgiveness of delinquent meal debt, and relief from collecting unpaid charges, while giving up paid-meal fee revenue.
